docs.title: ADR 011: Monorepo Strategy for Protocol Ecosystem
docs.text:
Status: Accepted Date: 2026-01-24 Deciders: Ryan Bumstead

Note: The packages this record refers to (glassspec, control-plane, adapters, and the Reference Console) are not part of this repository. The decision text is kept as history. The runtime package it names was replaced by the glassops CLI.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
GlassOps is a "Protocol Ecosystem" consisting of:

  1. The Law (glassspec) - The Interface
  2. The Manual (glassops/docs) - The Documentation
  3. The Implementations (runtime, control-plane, adapters) - The Code

The development team is currently one person.

docs.title: The Problem with Polyrepos (Separate Repos)
docs.text:
If we split these into 5+ repositories (glass-protocol, glass-runtime, glass-adapter-native, etc.):

  1. Context Switching Cost: Updating a standard requires 5 PRs across 5 repos.
  2. Versioning Hell: "Runtime v1.2 depends on Protocol v1.1 but imports Adapter v1.0 which expects Protocol v1.0."
  3. Synchronization Lag: The docs will inevitably drift from the code because they live in different universes.

For a solo developer, this friction is fatal.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: We will use a Single Governance Monorepo (glassops-platform/glassops) for all core components.

docs.title: The Structure
docs.text:
glassops/
├── packages/
│   ├── glassspec/              # The constraints (Sarif schemas, Protocol.md)
│   ├── runtime/                # The machinery (@glassops/runtime)
│   ├── control-plane/          # The brains (@glassops/control-plane)
│   └── adapters/               # The hands (@glassops/native-adapter, etc)
├── docs/                       # The Manual
└── config/                     # Shared configuration

docs.title: The "Publisher Pattern" for Distribution
docs.text:
While development happens in the Monorepo, consumption may require separate repos (e.g., GitHub Actions marketplace limitations).

Strategy:

  1. Develop in glassops.
  2. Release via automated pipelines that copy folders to read-only public mirrors (e.g., glassops-platform/glassops-runtime).
  3. Never write code in the mirrors.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
1. Atomic Protocol Updates: A single commit can update the SARIF spec in glassspec AND the implementation in glassops-runtime. Drift is impossible.
  2. Solo Velocity: Zero context switching. grep across the entire universe. Refactor global names in one pass.
  3. Coherent Versioning: The ecosystem moves forward together.

docs.title: Strategic Extensibility
docs.text: The monorepo structure allows for seamless expansion. we can add glassops-cli, glassops-docs, glassops-policy-engine, or even a second platform later without renaming anything. The structure is designed to accept new domains as top-level directories without disrupting the core.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Positive: Maximum velocity for 1-3 developers. Guaranteed consistency.
  • Negative: CI pipelines are complex (need to detect which folder changed).
  • Mitigation: Use tools like turborepo or simple path-based GitHub Action triggers.

Author: Ryan Bumstead (Population: 1)

docs.title: Alternatives
docs.text: • None considered.

docs.title: GlassOps Architecture & Design
docs.text: Target design. Only part of the glassops CLI exists today. The rest of this page describes intent, not working code. The GitHub Action runtime that this page once described was replaced by the CLI.

docs.title: 1. High-Level Architecture
docs.text: GlassOps is designed container-first. CI (GitHub Actions today) holds secrets and starts the run, and the glassops container decides whether the run may proceed.

docs.title: The Control Loop
docs.text:
graph LR
    Intent[User Intent] --> Policy[Policy Check]
    Policy -->|Approved| Exec[Deployment Step]
    Exec -->|Contract| Audit[Audit Trail]
    Policy -->|Rejected| Block[Block Deployment]

docs.title: Component Breakdown
docs.text:
1. CI (GitHub Actions): Owns secrets and starts the run.
  2. glassops CLI (partly built): Plans the change set, evaluates policy, signs a PERMIT, and deploys only under a valid PERMIT. See the CLI reference.
  3. Deployment step (not built): Executes the deploy and normalizes its output.
  4. Record format (not built): The message format (SARIF/OTel) exchanged between components.

docs.title: 2. Governance Flow (The Pipeline)
docs.text:
The target flow is four phases. The CLI implements parts of phases 1 to 4.

  1. Phase 1: Policy Resolution

    • Today the policy comes from glassops.yaml only.
    • Target: merge GitHub Vars (Floor) + devops-config.json (Team) + Salesforce CMDT (Additive) into one Effective Policy.

  2. Phase 2: Architectural Validity

    • Today gate evaluates the v1 rules over the plan, the CI context and earlier results. See PERMIT and rules.
    • Target: enforce Hard Invariants (e.g., No RunAllTests in Prod).

  3. Phase 3: Simulation (The Dry Run)

    • Partly built. validate runs a check-only deploy. Target: also generate a Draft Contract.

  4. Phase 4: Execution Gate

    • Partly built. gate signs a PERMIT and deploy refuses to run without a valid one. Target: compare the Draft Contract with the Effective Policy.

docs.title: Confused Deputy Protection
docs.text:
Principle: Salesforce never holds deployment secrets. CI holds secrets and authenticates to Salesforce with the JWT flow.

  • Benefit: If Salesforce is compromised, they cannot deploy to other envs. If GitHub is compromised, scope is limited to the specific repo environment.

docs.title: Secrets Management
docs.text:
• Location: GitHub Secrets (Environment Scoped).
  • Rotation: Not automated. Rotate JWT keys on your own schedule.

docs.title: 4. Failure Modes & Recovery
docs.text: Failure Behavior Recovery GitHub Down Deployment Impossible Manual sf deploy from local machine (Break Glass) Salesforce Down Workflow Fails Gracefully Retry when service restored Policy Block Workflow Fails (Intentional) Fix code or Request Manual Override

docs.title: 5. Directory Structure
docs.text: • cmd/glassops and internal/: The glassops CLI. This is the only code with working behaviour.

docs.title: Deploy with GitHub
docs.text:
Early work. v0.3.0 is released as a prerelease. The reusable workflows, the run command and the other new commands this guide uses ship in the next release.

This guide sets up pull request checks and a deploy to production on GitHub. Two reusable workflows in this repository run the glassops container image for you. Your repository calls them with a few lines each. examples/consumer/ is the smallest working layout, and glassops init writes a similar glassops.yaml and workflow into your project. For what a PERMIT is, see PERMIT and rules.

Reusable workflow Runs Triggered by glassops-pr.yml glassops run pr pull_request glassops-deploy.yml glassops run deploy, in a protected environment a push to main

The pipelines are the ones in your glassops.yaml. See Run a pipeline for the defaults.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A glassops.yaml with a Dev Hub target and a target named prod with tier prod, each with a login. See the configuration reference and Authentication.
  • The Salesforce secrets your targets name, such as SF_JWT_KEY, SF_CLIENT_ID, SF_USERNAME, SF_DEVHUB_ORG_ID, SF_PROD_USERNAME and SF_PROD_ORG_ID, as repository secrets.
  • A GitHub environment named glassops-deploy. Give it required reviewers if you want an approval before the deploy job runs, and a deployment branch rule that allows main only. The run's approval is read as evidence for the separation of duties rule.
  • The signing key GLASSOPS_PERMIT_KEY as a secret of that environment, not of the repository. Make one with openssl rand -base64 48. It must decode to at least 32 bytes.

The key must never be available to pull request jobs. Anyone who can run a job with the key can sign an allow PERMIT. A secret held only in the glassops-deploy environment reaches only jobs that name that environment, and you control which branches may use it. glassops doctor warns when GLASSOPS_PERMIT_KEY is set on a pull_request or pull_request_target run.

docs.title: Pull requests
docs.text:
Save this as .github/workflows/pr.yml:

name: glassops pr

on:
  pull_request:

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  glassops:
    uses: glassops-platform/glassops/.github/workflows/glassops-pr.yml@v1
    permissions:
      contents: read
      pull-requests: read
      security-events: write
    with:
      targets: devhub
    secrets:
      SF_JWT_KEY: ${{ secrets.SF_JWT_KEY }}
      SF_CLIENT_ID: ${{ secrets.SF_CLIENT_ID }}
      SF_USERNAME: ${{ secrets.SF_USERNAME }}
      SF_DEVHUB_ORG_ID: ${{ secrets.SF_DEVHUB_ORG_ID }}
      SF_PROD_USERNAME: ${{ secrets.SF_PROD_USERNAME }}
      SF_PROD_ORG_ID: ${{ secrets.SF_PROD_ORG_ID }}

The workflow checks out full history, runs glassops run pr, uploads the SARIF file to code scanning, and keeps the results as an artifact. It never receives the permit key.

Input Default Meaning image ghcr.io/glassops-platform/glassops:v1 The container image. Pass the glassops-analyzer image when analyze.enabled is true targets Space separated target names to log in to before the pipeline, so a bad login fails early upload-sarif true Upload the SARIF file. Needs code scanning on the repository

docs.title: Deploy
docs.text:
Save this as .github/workflows/deploy.yml:

name: glassops deploy

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  glassops:
    uses: glassops-platform/glassops/.github/workflows/glassops-deploy.yml@v1
    permissions:
      contents: write
      actions: read
      issues: read
      pull-requests: read
    with:
      environment: glassops-deploy
    secrets:
      GLASSOPS_PERMIT_KEY: ${{ secrets.GLASSOPS_PERMIT_KEY }}
      SF_JWT_KEY: ${{ secrets.SF_JWT_KEY }}
      SF_CLIENT_ID: ${{ secrets.SF_CLIENT_ID }}
      SF_USERNAME: ${{ secrets.SF_USERNAME }}
      SF_DEVHUB_ORG_ID: ${{ secrets.SF_DEVHUB_ORG_ID }}
      SF_PROD_USERNAME: ${{ secrets.SF_PROD_USERNAME }}
      SF_PROD_ORG_ID: ${{ secrets.SF_PROD_ORG_ID }}

glassops-deploy.yml takes the inputs image, environment (default glassops-deploy) and targets, like the pull request workflow.

The permit key is passed by name. The caller must list GLASSOPS_PERMIT_KEY under secrets, because a called workflow does not see environment secrets unless the caller passes them. The workflow declares the secret required: true, so a caller that omits it fails. The value lives only as a secret of the protected glassops-deploy environment. Do not add it as a repository secret. The deploy job runs in that environment, so the reviewers and branch rules you set there apply to it.

Permissions. The calling job needs these, because a called workflow cannot hold more than its caller grants:

Permission Why contents: write The runner pushes the glassops/deployed/prod tag actions: read gate reads this run's environment approvals pull-requests: read gate reads the pull request behind the commit, its author and labels issues: read gate reads who added an approval label

docs.title: What the deploy job does
docs.text:
1. Checks out full history. A shallow clone is an error, never an empty plan.
  2. Installs a glassops command on the runner that runs the image with docker run --rm, one container per command, with the workspace mounted at /work. The checkout, the tag push and the uploads run on the runner, not in the container.
  3. Logs in to each target in targets, when set, with glassops doctor --auth --target <name>.
  4. Runs glassops run deploy. With the default pipeline that is plan --target prod, validate --target prod, gate --target prod, deploy --target prod and report.
  5. Pushes the deployed tag. deploy moves the git tag glassops/deployed/prod inside the container, but the container has no git credentials, so its own push is only a warning. A runner step after the container exits pushes the glassops/deployed/* tags with the checkout's credentials. Without that tag, the next plan has no record of this deploy and starts from the merge base instead.
  6. Runs glassops report (also after a failure), and uploads .glassops/results/, plan.json and permit.json as the glassops-deploy-evidence artifact.

One deploy runs at a time per environment. A queued deploy waits and is never cancelled.

docs.title: How the steps fit together
docs.text:
• Plan. With --target prod and no --from, plan starts from the glassops/deployed/prod tag. If that tag does not exist yet, this is the first deploy and the whole source is planned.
  • Validate. A check-only validate against prod. It records which plan it validated, so gate can bind it into the PERMIT.
  • Gate. Evaluates the rules and writes .glassops/permit.json. A deny exits 1, so the run stops here and the deploy never starts.
  • Deploy. Verifies the PERMIT, then logs in and deploys. When the PERMIT holds a passed validation of this plan, it quick deploys it.
  • Report. Runs after a failed step, writes the run summary and SARIF, and exits with the worst status of the results.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• The references say @v1. The v1 workflow tag and the :v1 image tag move only on a final 1.x release. Until one exists, replace @v1 with a release tag or a commit SHA, and set the image input to a version tag.
  • Separation of duties needs the rule in glassops.yaml. When the person who merges is also the pull request author, the rule fails unless an approval satisfies it. Set approval.environment: glassops-deploy so an approval of the environment satisfies the rule. See PERMIT and rules.
  • The container runs as root, so files it writes under .glassops/ are owned by root on the runner.
  • The warning about the tag push inside the container appears on every deploy. That is expected, because the runner step pushes the tag.

docs.title: Other CI systems and single commands
docs.text:
glassops is one binary, so any CI can run glassops run pr and glassops run deploy with the same glassops.yaml. On GitHub, the glassops-platform/glassops action runs one command in the container, for steps that do not fit a pipeline:

- uses: glassops-platform/glassops@v1
  with:
    command: doctor --auth --target prod
    env: |
      SF_JWT_KEY
      SF_CLIENT_ID
  env:
    SF_JWT_KEY: ${{ secrets.SF_JWT_KEY }}
    SF_CLIENT_ID: ${{ secrets.SF_CLIENT_ID }}

docs.title: Run a pipeline
docs.text: glassops run <pipeline> runs a whole list of steps from glassops.yaml in one command. It runs the same way on a laptop and in any CI system, so a pipeline you run locally is the one your CI runs. The commands it calls are described in the CLI reference.

docs.title: Run it locally
docs.text:
From the project root, with git, the Salesforce CLI, sfdx-git-delta and the environment variables your targets name:

glassops run pr --dry-run   # print the steps, run nothing
glassops run pr

--dry-run shows each step, its when and the global flags it receives. It writes nothing and removes nothing. A real run writes one result file per step to .glassops/results/, plus run.json for the whole run. The exit code is the worst of all steps: 0 pass, 1 a check or policy failed, 2 a tool error.

docs.title: Run it in CI
docs.text:
In any CI, run the same command in the glassops container image, or with a glassops binary on the runner:

docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/work" -w /work \
  -e SF_JWT_KEY -e SF_CLIENT_ID -e SF_USERNAME -e SF_DEVHUB_ORG_ID \
  ghcr.io/glassops-platform/glassops:<version> run pr

run is not in v0.3.0. Use the image of the next release, or one you build from this repository with docker build -t glassops ..

On GitHub, the reusable workflows do this for you and add the checkout, the SARIF upload and the evidence upload. See Deploy with GitHub. For a single command outside a pipeline, the glassops-platform/glassops action takes command: run pr or any other command line.

docs.title: The default pipelines
docs.text:
A project with no glassops.yaml gets these two pipelines, exactly as config.DefaultPipelines() returns them. glassops init writes them into the file it creates. A glassops.yaml that has no pipelines key has none, and one that has the key uses only what it lists.

pipelines:
  pr:
    - plan
    - check
    - analyze
    - env create
    - validate --target ephemeral --fallback-target prod
    - step: report
      when: always
    - step: env delete
      when: always
  deploy:
    - plan --target prod
    - validate --target prod
    - gate --target prod
    - deploy --target prod
    - step: report
      when: always

pr. Plans the change, runs your project scripts (check), runs the Code Analyzer (analyze), creates a short-lived scratch org named ephemeral from the Dev Hub (env create), and runs a check-only validate there. --fallback-target prod makes validate use the prod target when no environment exists, for example when environments.ephemeral is not configured. report and env delete run even after a failure, so the run always leaves a summary and never leaves an org behind. validate runs the tests at the configured test level. To run the tests with coverage minimums as a separate step, add test --target ephemeral after validate.

deploy. Plans from what prod last received (--target prod starts from the glassops/deployed/prod tag), validates, asks the policy rules for a signed PERMIT, and deploys under it. A denied gate exits 1 and the deploy step is skipped. report runs either way. The deploy needs GLASSOPS_PERMIT_KEY, which should be available only to the protected deploy job. See Deploy with GitHub.

Two steps skip themselves when they have nothing to do. check does nothing without check.scripts, and analyze does nothing without analyze.enabled: true. Both end with the status empty and exit 0.

docs.title: Write your own
docs.text:
A step is a glassops command line without the glassops prefix, or a map. Add when to decide what runs after a failure, and an exec step to run any shell command.

pipelines:
  pr:
    - plan
    - step: exec
      run: npm run build
    - env create
    - validate --target ephemeral
    - test --target ephemeral
    - step: report
      when: always
    - step: env delete
      when: always
when The step runs success (the default) Only when no earlier step failed failure Only when an earlier step failed always Every time, including after a failure or a cancel

How run treats the steps:

  • Empty plan. After plan writes an empty plan, every later step that is not when: always is skipped. A pull request that changes no deployable source passes without logging in anywhere. A plan that cannot be read is an error, never an empty plan.
  • Failure. A step fails when its exit code is not 0. Later success steps are skipped. failure and always steps still run. The run exits with the worst code.
  • Exec steps. An exec step runs sh -c in the project directory. It gets GLASSOPS_RESULTS_DIR, the absolute path of the results directory, so a script can read or add to the results. Any non-zero exit is a fail. A command that cannot start is an error. The result is exec.<n>.json, with n counting exec steps from 1.
  • Same flags everywhere. Every glassops step receives the run's --dir, --config, --results-dir and --ci.
  • Stale results. A real run first removes run.json and the glassops result files left in the results directory by an earlier run, and keeps everything else. A report step cannot read an old run as evidence for this one.
  • Cancel. Ctrl+C or SIGTERM stops the current step, skips the rest, and still runs the when: always steps. The run exits at least 2.

A created environment is used automatically by later steps. env create writes .glassops/env/ephemeral/env.json and a login file, and validate --target ephemeral finds them. See env create.

docs.title: CLI Reference
docs.text:
Early work. v0.3.0 is released as a prerelease. It has init, doctor, describe, plan, validate, gate, permit verify, deploy and report. The commands env, test, run, check and analyze are in the repository and ship in the next release.

glassops is one Go binary that runs each delivery step as its own command. The goal is a governed pipeline that runs the same way in any CI system or on a laptop. Salesforce is the first provider.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text: Command What it does glassops init Detects the provider and the CI system, then writes glassops.yaml and a CI file glassops doctor Checks the config, the tools, the git checkout and the environment variables the config names. With --auth it also logs in to targets glassops describe Logs in to one target, runs the guard, and records what the target reports about itself glassops plan Works out what changed between two git refs and writes the manifests and a change set glassops validate Runs a check-only validate of the change set against a target glassops gate Evaluates the policy rules for a target and writes a signed PERMIT glassops permit verify Checks that a PERMIT is signed, unexpired and bound to this target, commit, plan and config glassops deploy Deploys the change set to a target, only under a valid PERMIT glassops report Summarises every result for the CI and writes SARIF glassops env create Creates the ephemeral environment (a scratch org) that later steps use glassops env delete Deletes that environment glassops env sweep Deletes old environments that a cancelled run left behind glassops test Runs Apex tests with coverage on a target and writes JUnit XML glassops run Runs a whole pipeline from glassops.yaml glassops check Runs your own project scripts glassops analyze Runs the Code Analyzer and records the violation counts

docs.title: glassops init
docs.text:
• Detects a Salesforce project from sfdx-project.json.
  • Detects the CI system from the project files (.github, bitbucket-pipelines.yml, .gitlab-ci.yml, azure-pipelines.yml) or from the environment it runs in.
  • Writes glassops.yaml with commented stub targets and the default pr and deploy pipelines.
  • For GitHub, also writes .github/workflows/glassops.yml, which runs glassops doctor on full git history. Other CI systems are detected but get no CI file yet.
  • Never overwrites a file unless you pass --force.

docs.title: glassops doctor
docs.text:
Runs these checks and fails if any of them fails:

  • glassops.yaml, when present, against the schema and its rules. Without the file, the defaults are used.
  • The provider: the config and the project files must agree.
  • The tools: git always, plus sf and the sfdx-git-delta plugin for Salesforce projects. Versions are recorded.
  • The analyzer, only when analyze.enabled is true: Java 11 or newer and the Code Analyzer plugin (tool.java and tool.code-analyzer). Both are in the glassops-analyzer image.
  • The checkout: a shallow clone fails, because it would make every change set empty. On GitHub, use actions/checkout with fetch-depth: 0.
  • The environment: every $VAR the config names must be set. Only presence is checked. Values are never printed or stored.
  • The PERMIT key: on a pull_request or pull_request_target run, GLASSOPS_PERMIT_KEY should not be set. If it is, doctor adds a permit.key check whose detail starts with warning: and a CI warning annotation. This never fails the command. Only presence is checked. See PERMIT and rules.

docs.title: glassops doctor --auth
docs.text:
Adds a login to each target in the config, or only the one named by --target, and runs the guard on it. Without --auth, doctor never logs in. The environment check covers every $VAR the config names. With --auth --target, it covers only that target's variables, so a target that does not exist yet, such as a scratch org that a later step creates, does not fail the check.

Flag Meaning --auth Also log in to targets and run the guard --target With --auth, check only this target

docs.title: glassops describe
docs.text:
Logs in to one target, runs the guard, and writes what the target reports about itself to .glassops/results/describe.json. A guard mismatch exits 2 before anything else runs.

Flag Meaning --target Target name from glassops.yaml (required)

docs.title: glassops plan
docs.text:
Works out the change set between two git refs. It writes the provider's manifests to .glassops/plan/ and the change set to .glassops/plan.json. For Salesforce, sfdx-git-delta works out the delta and the project's .forceignore applies. A shallow clone is an error, never an empty plan. With salesforce.delta.enabled: false, plan lists the whole source instead, and it reads no git history.

Flag Default Meaning --from auto Base git ref, or auto --to auto Head git ref, or auto (HEAD) --target Target the plan is for, used by --from auto

With --from auto, a pull request uses the merge base with its base branch. With --target, auto uses the git tag glassops/deployed/<target>, then the merge base with the target's branch. Without either, pass --from.

First deploy rule: with --target and --from auto, a target that has no glassops/deployed/<target> tag has never received a deploy from glassops. plan then plans the whole source instead of a delta, prints a notice, and records the facts plan.first_deploy and plan.from_source: first-deploy. A shallow clone is still an error.

docs.title: glassops validate
docs.text:
Logs in to the target, runs the guard, and runs a check-only validate of the change set in .glassops/plan.json. It never deploys. See Validate is check-only.

Flag Default Meaning --target Target name from glassops.yaml (required) --fallback-target Target to use when --target is not configured or not reachable --plan <dir>/.glassops/plan.json Change set file --check-only true Always true. false is refused

A target counts as not configured when it is missing from glassops.yaml or when its id variable is not set, for example because the scratch org was never created. A guard mismatch never falls back. The test level comes from salesforce.test_level for the tier of the target used, then its default entry, then the Salesforce CLI's own default. An empty change set ends with status empty and no login. validate records the facts validate.plan_sha256 and validate.test_level, which gate uses to decide whether a deploy may reuse the validation. See validation binding.

docs.title: glassops gate
docs.text:
Reads the change set, the earlier results in the results directory and the CI context. It builds the facts for one target, runs the policy rules over them, and writes a signed PERMIT to .glassops/permit.json. It writes the PERMIT whether the answer is allow or deny, and it deletes any PERMIT already at that path first, so an old allow never survives a failed run. Unless --no-connect is set, it logs in to the target and runs the guard. The rules, the PERMIT and the evidence gate reads are described in PERMIT and rules.

Flag Default Meaning --target Target name from glassops.yaml (required) --plan <dir>/.glassops/plan.json Change set file --permit <dir>/.glassops/permit.json Where the PERMIT is written --no-connect false Do not log in. The PERMIT records the configured Id and the kind the guard requires for the tier, and the guard check is skipped

Needs GLASSOPS_PERMIT_KEY. Reads .glassops/plan.json, .glassops/results/plan.json and .glassops/results/validate.json when they exist, and the CI context. Writes .glassops/permit.json, .glassops/facts.json and .glassops/results/gate.json.

Exit When 0 The PERMIT allows the deploy 1 Policy denies the deploy. The signed PERMIT is still written 2 GLASSOPS_PERMIT_KEY is missing or unusable, the plan file is missing or unreadable, the target is not in the config, or evidence could not be gathered. A missing key, plan or target writes no PERMIT. Evidence that could not be gathered writes a signed PERMIT that denies

Result facts: gate.allow, gate.ephemeral, gate.permit_id and gate.expires_at.

docs.title: glassops permit verify
docs.text:
Checks a PERMIT without logging in to the target, so any deploy tool can honour it. It checks the key, the signature, that the PERMIT allows, that it has not expired, and that it matches the target, the commit, the plan and the config. The order is in PERMIT and rules.

Flag Default Meaning --target Target name from glassops.yaml (required) --permit <dir>/.glassops/permit.json PERMIT file --plan <dir>/.glassops/plan.json Change set file

Needs GLASSOPS_PERMIT_KEY. Reads the PERMIT, the change set, the plan files under .glassops/plan/, glassops.yaml and the CI commit. Writes .glassops/results/permit-verify.json.

Exit When 0 The PERMIT holds 1 The PERMIT does not hold: bad signature, denied, expired, a different target, commit, plan or config, a file that is not a readable PERMIT, or plan files changed after plan 2 The key is missing or unusable, or the PERMIT file, the change set, the config or the commit cannot be read or found

Result facts: permit.key_id, permit.id and permit.expires_at.

docs.title: glassops deploy
docs.text:
Verifies the PERMIT before it logs in. Then it runs the guard and deploys the change set in .glassops/plan.json. When the PERMIT holds a validated deploy Id, it quick deploys that validation. See validation binding. Success is read from the target's result body. After a successful deploy it moves the git tag glassops/deployed/<target> to the deployed commit and pushes it. The tag is lightweight. A failed move or push is a warning, because the deploy has already happened: the tag check is skipped, deploy.tag_pushed is false, and the CI gets a warning annotation.

Flag Default Meaning --target Target name from glassops.yaml (required) --plan <dir>/.glassops/plan.json Change set file --permit <dir>/.glassops/permit.json PERMIT file --wait the provider's How long to wait for the deploy, such as 30m. The Salesforce provider waits 60 minutes --resume Job Id of an earlier deploy to wait on again. Skips quick deploy

Needs GLASSOPS_PERMIT_KEY. The deployed commit is the CI's commit, or git rev-parse HEAD when the CI reports none. It must be the commit the PERMIT names. An empty change set under a valid PERMIT ends with status empty and no login.

Exit When 0 The deploy succeeded, or the change set was empty 1 The deploy ran and the target reported failures, or salesforce.deploy.quick is require and the PERMIT holds no passed validation to quick deploy 2 The PERMIT is missing, unreadable, denied, expired or does not match, the plan files changed, login or the guard failed, or the deploy did not finish within --wait. A timeout keeps the job Id and prints the --resume command, and does not move the tag

Result facts: deploy.permit_id, deploy.quick_mode, deploy.id, deploy.quick, deploy.timed_out, deploy.commit, deploy.tag and deploy.tag_pushed, plus the provider's own facts.

docs.title: glassops report
docs.text:
Reads every result in the results directory. It writes a markdown summary to the CI's run summary, and with --summary also to a file. It writes SARIF to --sarif for policy denials found in the PERMIT and for failed checks in the validate and deploy results. SARIF files already in the results directory, such as Code Analyzer's, are merged into the output. The SARIF file it writes is skipped when it reads the directory again. report writes no result file of its own.

Flag Default Meaning --sarif <dir>/.glassops/report.sarif SARIF file to write --summary Also write the markdown summary to this file

report exits with the worst status among the results: 0 when all pass, 1 when any failed, 2 when any errored. That lets a CI run it after a failed step with if: always() and still fail the job. It also exits 2 when there are no results or one cannot be read.

docs.title: glassops env create
docs.text:
Creates the ephemeral environment named under environments in glassops.yaml, from its Dev Hub target, for later steps to use. It logs in to the hub and runs the guard on it. The default pr pipeline runs it before validate.

For Salesforce it does not run sf org create scratch. It creates a ScratchOrgInfo record in the Dev Hub (a signup), polls until the record is Active for up to 15 minutes, and exchanges the record's auth code for a login. A signup refused for capacity or a transient error is retried up to three times. A signup that is still not active after 15 minutes is not retried, because it could still become active. The scratch definition file (environments.<target>.definition) supports the keys edition, features, hasSampleData, language, country, description, release and sourceOrg. Any other key, including settings, is an error, so an org is never created without something the file asks for. orgName is replaced by the environment name.

Flag Default Meaning --target ephemeral Environment name from the environments section --name <prefix>-<repo>-<pr or branch>-<run> Environment name. The prefix is environments.<target>.prefix, default glassops. Outside CI the repo is the project directory and the run is a UTC timestamp --ttl-days environments.<target>.ttl_days, else 1 Days the environment lives --shape environments.<target>.shape Source org Id for an org shape. A $VAR is read from the environment --env-file <dir>/.glassops/env/<target>/env.json Where to write env.json

How later steps use the org. env create writes env.json and a login file. env.json records the environment name, Id, expiry and the path of the login file, and holds no secret. The login file holds an sfdx-url login, is readable only by the current user, and lives in the operating system's temporary directory. When each command runs in its own container, set TMPDIR to a mount they share. A later command that resolves a target named under environments, such as validate --target ephemeral, finds env.json and logs in with that file instead of the $VAR settings. With no env.json, the target falls back to its targets entry, and --fallback-target applies if that is not configured. An env.json that records a failed create (ready: false) counts as not configured. On GitHub, env create also sets the step outputs env_id, env_file and auth_file.

env create refuses to run when env.json already exists, so run env delete first. If the create fails after the signup was requested, env.json is still written so env delete can remove the org.

Writes .glassops/results/env-create.json with the facts env.file, env.id, env.record_id, env.name, env.auth_file and env.expires_at, plus the provider's own.

Exit When 0 The environment is active 2 environments.<target> is not configured, env.json already exists, the hub login or guard failed, or the signup failed or timed out

docs.title: glassops env delete
docs.text:
Deletes the environment from its hub. It reads env.json, or finds the environment by --name. With neither, nothing is recorded to delete: the delete check is skipped and the command exits 0. Deleting an environment that is already gone passes. After a delete from env.json, it removes the login file and env.json, so later steps fall back to the config. The default pr pipeline runs it with when: always.

Flag Default Meaning --target ephemeral Environment name from the environments section --name the one env create made Delete by name instead of from env.json --env-file <dir>/.glassops/env/<target>/env.json env.json to read

Writes .glassops/results/env-delete.json. Exit 0 when the environment is deleted, already gone, or nothing is recorded. Exit 2 when the config, the hub login or env.json (for another target or hub) is wrong, or the delete fails.

docs.title: glassops env sweep
docs.text:
Deletes every environment on the hub whose name starts with <prefix>- and that is older than --max-age, and lists what it deleted. It never matches the bare prefix. Run it on a schedule to remove environments that a cancelled run left behind.

Flag Default Meaning --target ephemeral Environment name from the environments section, which supplies the hub and the prefix --max-age environments.<target>.ttl_days as a duration Delete environments older than this, such as 24h. Must be above zero

Writes .glassops/results/env-sweep.json with the facts env.prefix, env.max_age, env.deleted and env.deleted_count. Exit 0 when the sweep finished, 2 when the config, the hub login or a delete failed.

docs.title: glassops test
docs.text:
Logs in to the target, runs the guard, and runs the target's Apex tests with code coverage. It never deploys. It writes JUnit XML and checks the result against test.coverage.

Flag Default Meaning --target Target name from glassops.yaml (required) --level test.level for the target's tier, then test.level.default Test level, such as RunLocalTests --tests Comma separated tests to run, for a level that names them --wait the provider's How long to wait for the run, such as 30m --resume Run Id of an earlier run to wait on again, instead of starting a new one --junit <results-dir>/test.junit.xml JUnit XML file to write

Coverage. Percentages are rounded down, so a rounded-up value never passes a minimum. Both settings are optional:

  • test.coverage.org_min compares against the org-wide coverage that sf reports. That figure counts every class in the org, so it catches classes that no test touches.
  • test.coverage.class_min compares each class that the test run reports. test sees per-class coverage only for the classes in that report, so a class that no test ran against can be missing from it. Set org_min as well to catch those.

If a minimum is set and its figure is not reported, that is a failure, never a pass. A run that does not finish within --wait fails and names the run Id, and --resume waits on it again.

No tests found. When sf reports that no Apex tests were found, test records the fact test.none_found. It fails when org_min or class_min is set, because coverage cannot be checked. When neither is set, the status is empty, the tests check is skipped, and it exits 0.

Writes .glassops/results/test.json and the JUnit file (listed as an artifact). Facts: test.ran, test.failed, test.finished, test.run_id, test.org_coverage (a whole percent, absent when unknown), test.coverage.<Class>.percent and target.source.

Exit When 0 The tests passed and every set minimum is met, or no tests were found and no minimum is set 1 A test failed, the run did not finish, coverage is below a minimum or was not reported, or no tests ran while a minimum is set 2 The target could not be resolved, the login or guard failed, or the tests could not be run

docs.title: glassops run
docs.text:
Runs the steps of one pipeline from glassops.yaml, in order, in one process. See Run a pipeline for the default pipelines.

glassops run pr
glassops run deploy --dry-run
Flag Default Meaning --dry-run false Print the steps and the global flags each one gets. Runs nothing and removes nothing

A step is a glassops command line such as validate --target prod, or a map with step, when and, for an exec step, run.

When a step runs. when decides what happens after an earlier step failed.

when The step runs success (the default) Only when no earlier step failed failure Only when an earlier step failed always Every time, including after a failure or a cancel

A step has failed when its exit code is not 0. After a plan step that exits 0, run reads .glassops/plan.json. An empty plan skips every later step that is not when: always, with the reason "the plan is empty". A plan that cannot be read is an error (exit 2), and later success steps are skipped, so it is never read as an empty plan. A cancel (Ctrl+C or SIGTERM) stops the current step and skips the rest except when: always steps, which still run with up to 2 minutes each. A cancelled run exits at least 2.

Exec steps. A step named exec runs its run command with sh -c in the project directory. The command inherits the environment and gets GLASSOPS_RESULTS_DIR, the absolute path of the results directory. Its output goes straight to the run's output. A zero exit passes and any other exit is a fail (exit 1). A command that cannot start, is stopped by a signal or is cancelled is an error (exit 2). Each exec step writes exec.<n>.json, where n counts exec steps from 1, with one command check and the facts exec.run, exec.index and exec.exit_code.

Global flags. Every glassops step receives this run's --dir, --config, --results-dir and --ci, so all steps read one project and write to one results directory.

Stale results. Before the first step, a real run removes run.json and every top-level *.json file in the results directory whose schema is glassops.result/v1. It does not recurse and keeps every other file, such as SARIF and JUnit files. This stops an earlier run from reading as evidence for this one. The count is the fact run.stale_removed. A removal failure exits 2 before any step runs.

Exit code. The worst exit code of all steps. Any code other than 0 and 1 ranks as 2.

Writes .glassops/results/run.json with the facts run.pipeline, run.steps (index, step, when, argv, result, exit code, duration, skip reason), run.exit_code, run.empty_plan, run.cancelled and run.stale_removed, and one check per step. A pipeline that is not in the config, or a step that does not parse, exits 2 before anything runs.

docs.title: glassops check
docs.text:
Runs your own project scripts, such as lint or unit test commands, and records the outcome. It does not replace those tools.

Scripts come from check.scripts in glassops.yaml, a list of name and run entries. Each runs with sh -c in the project directory, in order, and every script runs even after an earlier one failed. A script's output goes to the log and never into the result.

Flag Default Meaning --script Run only the script with this name. An unknown name is an error

Writes .glassops/results/check.json with one check per script named script.<name> and the facts check.scripts, check.passed and check.failed. With no scripts configured the status is empty and the exit code is 0.

Exit When 0 Every script exited 0, or none are configured 1 A script exited non-zero 2 sh could not start, or --script names no entry

docs.title: glassops analyze
docs.text:
Runs the Salesforce Code Analyzer over the project and records how many violations it found. It runs only when analyze.enabled: true is set in glassops.yaml. Without that, it records a skipped check, the status empty, and exits 0.

The analyzer needs Java 11 or newer and the Code Analyzer plugin of the Salesforce CLI. The standard glassops image has neither, so run analyze in the separate glassops-analyzer image, which adds them. glassops doctor checks for Java and the plugin when analyze.enabled is true. Only the Salesforce provider is supported.

Flag Default Meaning --rule-selector analyze.rule_selector, else Recommended Rules to run --sarif <results-dir>/analyze.sarif SARIF file to write

analyze does not decide what is too severe. It exits 0 whatever it found, so long as the analyzer ran. The gate rule analyzer_max_severity reads the counts and decides. It writes .glassops/results/analyze.json with the facts analyze.rule_selector, analyze.total and analyze.sev1 to analyze.sev5. The SARIF file and the analyzer's own JSON (.glassops/analyze/code-analyzer.json, beside the results directory) are listed as artifacts, and report merges the SARIF file into its output.

Exit When 0 The analyzer ran, or analyze is off 2 The analyzer could not run, its output could not be read, or the provider is not Salesforce

docs.title: The smart seed
docs.text:
A destructive change, such as a deleted field, cannot be validated on a fresh scratch org, because the component it deletes was never there. When validate runs against a scratch org and the change set has destructive members, it first deploys the base state they need. The base ref is the plan's from ref. salesforce.ephemeral.seed chooses how:

Mode What it deploys minimal (the default) Only the destructive members, from the base ref, plus the parent object of any child component (field, record type, validation rule and similar) whose parent is a custom object (__c, __mdt or __e) full The whole source at the base ref off Nothing. The destructive change is validated against the org as it is

If a minimal seed fails because something else is missing (an error such as Entity 'Widget__c' not found), the seed falls back to the full seed, records validate.seed.fallback: true and raises a CI warning. A failed seed stops validate before it runs. The seed applies to scratch targets only. validate records validate.seed.mode, validate.seed.fallback and validate.seed.members.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
Each target names its login under auth. There are three methods, and every secret value is a $VAR that names an environment variable. Values stay in your CI's secret store and never go in the file.

Method Fields Notes jwt username, client_id, key, optional instance_url key is a $VAR that holds the private key as PEM text. A value that is not PEM text is read as the path of a key file sfdx-url url url is a $VAR that holds a force:// auth URL access-token token, instance_url token is a $VAR that holds an access token 
targets:
  devhub:
    id: $SF_DEVHUB_ORG_ID
    tier: devhub
    auth: { method: jwt, username: $SF_USERNAME, client_id: $SF_CLIENT_ID, key: $SF_JWT_KEY }
  ephemeral:
    id: $SF_EPHEMERAL_ORG_ID
    tier: ephemeral
    auth: { method: sfdx-url, url: $SF_EPHEMERAL_AUTH_URL }

docs.title: Isolated Salesforce CLI state
docs.text: Every command that talks to an org runs the Salesforce CLI with its own temporary home directory (HOME and USERPROFILE). It never reads or writes the Salesforce CLI logins you have on your machine. The temporary directory, and any key file written into it, is removed when the command ends, including when it is stopped with Ctrl+C or SIGTERM. Logins are retried only on network and server errors, never on a bad key, an unknown user or an expired token.

docs.title: The guard
docs.text:
Before any step does anything to a target, the guard compares the org the login reached with the target in the config. A mismatch exits 2.

  • The Id is compared on its first 15 characters, case-sensitively, so a 15 and an 18 character form of one Id match.
  • A target with no Id configured fails, because it cannot be checked.
  • Tier prod and tier devhub need a production org.
  • Tier ephemeral needs a scratch org.
  • Every other tier checks the Id only.

docs.title: What is never logged
docs.text: Results, step outputs, CI annotations and error messages never contain the org's company name, tokens, private keys, auth URLs or full usernames. Usernames are masked to their first character and domain, such as u***@example.com. Email-shaped text in a tool's error message is masked the same way.

docs.title: Validate is check-only
docs.text: validate is check-only by construction. It only ever runs sf project deploy validate, never a deploy, and --check-only=false is refused. After the run it reads the full result with sf project deploy report and exits 2 if the target reports anything other than a check-only run. Keep a Dev Hub for managing scratch orgs, and validate against a scratch org or a sandbox.

docs.title: Global flags
docs.text: Flag Default Meaning --dir . Project root --config <dir>/glassops.yaml Config file --results-dir <dir>/.glassops/results Where results are written --ci auto CI system: auto, github or local

docs.title: Exit codes
docs.text: Code Meaning 0 Pass 1 A policy or check failed. The tool itself worked 2 A tool or infrastructure error stopped the command, or the command line was invalid

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
Every command writes .glassops/results/<step>.json in one envelope, described by schemas/result.json:

{
  "schema": "glassops.result/v1",
  "step": "doctor",
  "status": "pass",
  "started": "2026-10-26T12:00:00Z",
  "ended": "2026-10-26T12:00:02Z",
  "provider": "salesforce",
  "checks": [{ "name": "tool.sf", "status": "pass", "detail": "2.155.7" }],
  "facts": { "tools.sf": "2.155.7" },
  "artifacts": [],
  "errors": []
}

status is one of pass, fail, error, skipped or empty.

On GitHub, each command also sets the step outputs status and result (the result file path), adds an error annotation for each failed check, and writes a table to the job summary.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: glassops.yaml is optional. Every key, with an example, is in the configuration reference. The schema is schemas/config.json.

docs.title: End-to-end check
docs.text: The workflow cli-e2e.yml creates a scratch org in a Dev Hub, runs doctor --auth, plan and validate against it, and deletes the org. It runs on demand and on pushes to main, and it skips with a notice when the Salesforce secrets are not set. The scripts are in scripts/e2e.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
v0.3.0 is released as a prerelease, with a container image at ghcr.io/glassops-platform/glassops:0.3.0. The image adds Node 22, the Salesforce CLI and sfdx-git-delta. The commands env, test, run, check and analyze are not in v0.3.0. To use them now, build from a checkout with Go 1.27.3 or later:

go build -o glassops ./cmd/glassops
./glassops doctor

Or build the container image with docker build -t glassops . from the repository root. The analyze command needs the separate glassops-analyzer image, which adds Java and the Code Analyzer plugin. Build it with docker build -f Dockerfile.analyzer -t glassops-analyzer ..

docs.title: Configuration reference
docs.text:
glassops.yaml is optional. Without it, the commands use their defaults and the default pipelines. The schema is schemas/config.json. It rejects keys it does not know, so a typo is an error. glassops doctor validates the file.

Secrets are never written in the file. A secret field names an environment variable with a $VAR value, and the value stays in your CI's secret store.

Beyond the schema, these rules are checked:

  • Org Ids look like Salesforce org Ids, unless written as a $VAR.
  • No two targets share an org Id.
  • At most one target has tier prod.
  • Every policy window names a time zone that exists, and its from and to differ.
  • Every blackout has valid dates and ends on or after its start date.
  • policy.permit_ttl is a duration from 5 minutes to 24 hours.
  • A separation of duties approval sets environment or label, and a label needs approvers.
  • Every environments.<name>.devhub names a configured target.
  • No pipeline step is empty.

Names (targets, tiers, environments, pipelines) are lowercase letters, digits, _ and -, starting with a letter.

docs.title: Top-level keys
docs.text: Key Required What it holds version yes The schema version. Always 1 provider no salesforce. Detected from the project files when absent targets no Orgs that changes go to, with their login policy no Deploy windows, blackouts and the rules gate evaluates salesforce no Salesforce provider settings environments no Ephemeral environments that env create makes test no Test levels and coverage minimums for test check no Project scripts that check runs analyze no Code Analyzer settings pipelines no Named lists of steps for run

docs.title: version and provider
docs.text:
version: 1
provider: salesforce

docs.title: targets
docs.text:
One entry per org. The key is the target name that --target takes.

Field Meaning id The org Id the login must land on (the guard), or a $VAR holding it tier A name that policy windows, rules and test levels key on. prod, devhub and ephemeral have fixed meaning in the guard branch The git branch that deploys to this target. plan --from auto uses its merge base when the target has no deployed tag auth The login. See Authentication 
targets:
  devhub:
    id: $SF_DEVHUB_ORG_ID
    tier: devhub
    auth: { method: jwt, username: $SF_USERNAME, client_id: $SF_CLIENT_ID, key: $SF_JWT_KEY }
  prod:
    id: $SF_PROD_ORG_ID
    tier: prod
    branch: main
    auth: { method: jwt, username: $SF_PROD_USERNAME, client_id: $SF_CLIENT_ID, key: $SF_JWT_KEY }

docs.title: policy
docs.text:
What gate evaluates. The rules are described in PERMIT and rules.

Field Meaning windows Per tier, a list of allowed deploy windows: days, from, to (24 hour HH:MM) and tz (an IANA zone) blackouts Date ranges (from, to, optional tiers and reason) when no deploy is allowed rules coverage_min, analyzer_max_severity, separation_of_duties, destructive_needs_label permit_ttl How long a PERMIT stays valid, from 5m to 24h. The default is 2h actors Accepted by the schema. No command reads it yet 
policy:
  permit_ttl: 2h
  windows:
    prod: [{ days: [tue, thu], from: "18:00", to: "22:00", tz: America/Chicago }]
  blackouts:
    - { from: "2026-12-20", to: "2027-01-03", tiers: [prod], reason: holiday freeze }
  rules:
    coverage_min: 75
    analyzer_max_severity: 2
    destructive_needs_label: { label: destructive-ok, tiers: [prod] }
    separation_of_duties:
      tiers: [prod]
      approval: { environment: glassops-deploy }

docs.title: salesforce
environments
docs.text:
One entry per ephemeral environment, keyed by the target name the environment registers as. The default pr pipeline uses the name ephemeral. See env create.

Field Meaning devhub The target that creates the environment (required) definition Scratch definition file, relative to the project root ttl_days Days the environment lives. The default is 1 shape Source org Id for an org shape, or a $VAR holding one prefix Starts every environment name. The default is glassops 
environments:
  ephemeral:
    devhub: devhub
    definition: config/project-scratch-def.json
    ttl_days: 1

docs.title: test
docs.text:
Settings for glassops test.

Field Meaning level Map of tier to test level, with a default key. The --level flag overrides it coverage.org_min Minimum org-wide coverage, 0 to 100 coverage.class_min Minimum coverage for each class the test run reports, 0 to 100 
test:
  level: { default: RunLocalTests }
  coverage: { org_min: 75, class_min: 75 }

docs.title: check
docs.text:
Scripts that glassops check runs with sh -c.

check:
  scripts:
    - { name: lint, run: npm run lint }
    - { name: unit, run: npm test }

docs.title: analyze
docs.text:
Settings for glassops analyze. Nothing runs until enabled is true.

Field Meaning enabled true turns analyze on. It also needs the glassops-analyzer image rule_selector Code Analyzer rules to run. The default is Recommended max_severity The default for policy.rules.analyzer_max_severity, 1 (critical) to 5. The policy value wins when both are set 
analyze:
  enabled: true
  rule_selector: Recommended
  max_severity: 2

docs.title: pipelines
docs.text:
Named lists of steps for glassops run. Each step is a string (a glassops command line without the glassops prefix) or a map with step, optional when (success, failure or always) and, for the step exec, a run shell command. A pipeline needs at least one step.

pipelines:
  pr:
    - plan
    - check
    - step: exec
      run: npm run build
    - step: report
      when: always

The default pr and deploy pipelines apply only when the project has no glassops.yaml. A file that has a pipelines key replaces them, and one without the key has no pipelines, so glassops run pr fails with an unknown pipeline. glassops init writes the defaults into the file. See Run a pipeline.

docs.title: PERMIT and Rules
docs.text:
Early work. v0.3.0 is released as a prerelease and includes gate, permit verify and deploy. This page covers them.

A PERMIT is a signed file that records one decision: whether one plan may be deployed to one target. glassops gate makes the decision and writes the PERMIT. glassops deploy and glassops permit verify refuse to go on unless the PERMIT is genuine, still valid and about the thing being deployed. This page describes the PERMIT, the rules that feed it, and the evidence gate reads. The commands are in the CLI reference.

docs.title: What a PERMIT is
docs.text:
The PERMIT is JSON in .glassops/permit.json, with the schema name glassops.permit/v1. It holds:

Field Meaning id A random identifier, in hex allow true or false. A deny is recorded as a PERMIT too issued_at, expires_at When it was made and when it stops being valid. The lifetime is policy.permit_ttl target The target name, tier, id and kind. The Id and kind are what the login reported, unless --no-connect was used commit The commit the CI reported plan_sha256 The hash of the plan files config_sha256 The hash of glassops.yaml validation Optional. The deploy Id of a passed check-only validation, its test level and passed separation_of_duties How the separation of duties rule was met. See below checks Every rule result, each with its rule name, outcome and detail signature The algorithm, the key id and the signature value

A PERMIT binds to a specific target, commit, plan and config. Change any of them after gate ran and the PERMIT no longer matches.

docs.title: The signing key
docs.text:
The PERMIT is signed with HMAC-SHA256. The key comes from the environment variable GLASSOPS_PERMIT_KEY, which holds base64 text that decodes to at least 32 bytes. Standard base64 is accepted with or without padding. A shorter key is refused, and the error never contains the key. One way to make a key:

openssl rand -base64 48

The key_id in the signature is the first eight hex characters of the SHA-256 of the key. It names the key without revealing it. permit verify and deploy refuse a PERMIT whose key_id differs from their own key's, with the message that it was signed with a different key.

The signature covers the whole PERMIT, with the signature value left out: keys sorted, no extra whitespace, times in UTC. A PERMIT file with a field the format does not know, or with trailing data, is refused as unreadable, because such a field would not be covered by the signature.

The key must never be available to pull request jobs. Anyone who can run a job with the key can sign an allow. Put it in a protected CI environment that only the deploy job uses. glassops doctor adds a warning when GLASSOPS_PERMIT_KEY is set on a pull_request or pull_request_target run. See Deploy with GitHub.

docs.title: What gate does
docs.text:
gate always writes a signed PERMIT, including when policy denies the deploy. The deny is part of the record. Before it does anything else, it deletes any PERMIT already at the output path, so a stale allow can never stand in for the current run.

Two things stop it before a PERMIT is written, and both exit 2: GLASSOPS_PERMIT_KEY is missing or unusable, and the plan file or the target cannot be found. Everything after that still produces a signed PERMIT.

The checks in the PERMIT come in this order: the guard check, the validation.bound check, the rule results, then any evidence.* failures. The guard is the org Id and tier check described in the CLI reference. With --no-connect it does not run, the PERMIT records the configured Id and the kind the tier requires, and the guard check is skipped.

gate also writes the facts it evaluated to .glassops/facts.json.

docs.title: Fail closed
docs.text:
Missing evidence is never a pass.

  • A rule that needs a fact that is not there fails, or says so in its detail.
  • A tool or infrastructure problem while gathering evidence adds a failing evidence.<name> check. The PERMIT denies, is still signed and written, and gate exits 2 instead of 1. Examples: the guard refusing the target, a GitHub API call that fails, a result file that exists but cannot be read, a missing commit or plan hash, and plan files that no longer match the plan hash.
  • A rule set with no rules is a defect, never a pass.

docs.title: The ephemeral automatic PERMIT
docs.text: A target whose login the guard accepted as a scratch org gets an automatic PERMIT. Only the org Id guard applies. The rules are not run, no GitHub API call is made, and the PERMIT carries an ephemeral check and a not_applicable separation of duties record. It is issued only when the guard really ran and saw a scratch org, so --no-connect on an ephemeral target runs the full rule set instead. The result fact gate.ephemeral says which happened.

docs.title: What permit verify and deploy check
docs.text:
Both use the same verification, in this order. The first failure is the one reported.

permit verify, before the PERMIT checks:

  1. The key. A missing or unusable key is an error (exit 2) before anything else is read.
  2. The config, the target, the change set and the commit. A problem reading any of them is an error (exit 2).
  3. The PERMIT file. A missing file is an error (exit 2). A file that is not a readable PERMIT is a failure (exit 1).
  4. The plan files. If the files under .glassops/plan/ no longer hash to the change set's plan_sha256, the plan was edited after plan and the check fails (exit 1).

deploy, before the PERMIT checks, reads the target, the change set, the config hash and the commit, then checks the plan files the same way. In deploy every refusal is exit 2, because nothing may touch the target. The login comes after verification.

The PERMIT checks, shared by both:

  1. The signature: it exists, the algorithm is HMAC-SHA256, the key id matches, and the value verifies.
  2. The schema is glassops.permit/v1.
  3. allow is true.
  4. It has not expired.
  5. The target name matches.
  6. The target Id matches. Ids compare on their canonical form, so a 15 and an 18 character form of one Id are equal.
  7. The commit matches.
  8. The plan hash matches.
  9. The config hash matches.

Checking the signature first means a forged or damaged PERMIT is rejected before any of its contents are trusted. deploy additionally compares the PERMIT against the deployed commit, which is the CI's commit, or git rev-parse HEAD when the CI reports none.

docs.title: Validation binding and quick deploy
docs.text:
gate can bind a check-only validation into the PERMIT, so deploy can quick deploy it instead of deploying again. It binds the validation only when all of these hold for .glassops/results/validate.json:

  • The result passed.
  • It is for the same target name.
  • It was a check-only run with a deploy Id.
  • It records the plan hash it validated (validate.plan_sha256) and that hash equals the current plan.

The PERMIT then carries validation with the deploy Id and the recorded test level. The validation.bound check says whether it was bound and why not. It never denies. Without a bound validation, deploy runs a full deploy.

How deploy uses it depends on salesforce.deploy.quick in glassops.yaml:

Value Behaviour prefer (default) Quick deploy the bound validation. If the target refuses it, fall back to a full deploy and record salesforce.quick_refused require Quick deploy only. With no passed validation in the PERMIT, deploy fails with exit 1 before any login. If the target refuses the quick deploy, no full deploy runs off Always run a full deploy

The target refuses a quick deploy when the validation was never run, was already deployed, or is more than ten days old.

docs.title: The v1 rules
docs.text:
gate runs these seven rules, in this order. Every rule runs, so the PERMIT lists every reason for a deny. Only a fail outcome denies. The outcomes are pass, fail, skipped, waived_by_config and satisfied_by_approval.

Rule Outcomes plan_not_empty fail if the plan has no changes, or the facts do not say. Otherwise pass window.<tier> See below blackout See below coverage_min See below destructive_needs_label See below separation_of_duties See below analyzer_max_severity See below

docs.title: window.<tier>
docs.text:
Named after the target's tier, such as window.prod. Configured as policy.windows.<tier>, a list of weekly windows with days, from, to and tz.

  • skipped when no window is configured for the tier.
  • pass when now is inside any window for the tier.
  • fail when now is outside every window, or a window cannot be used (an unknown time zone or a bad clock).
  • fail, under the plain name window, when the tier is unknown and any window is configured anywhere.

Times are wall clock times in the window's zone, so the window moves with daylight saving time. A window is from up to but not including to. A window whose to is earlier than its from runs past midnight and belongs to the day it starts on. A window where from equals to never matches.

docs.title: blackout
docs.text:
Configured as policy.blackouts, a list with from and to dates (YYYY-MM-DD), optional tiers and an optional reason. Dates are compared in UTC, because a blackout has no time zone, and both ends are included.

  • skipped when no blackouts are configured.
  • fail when today (UTC) falls in a blackout that covers the target's tier. An empty tiers list covers every tier. When the tier is not known, every blackout in range counts.
  • pass otherwise.

docs.title: coverage_min
docs.text:
Configured as policy.rules.coverage_min, a whole number from 0 to 100.

  • skipped when it is not set.
  • fail when the plan facts do not list the changed Apex classes.
  • Otherwise it checks each changed Apex class against the per class coverage facts from the validate result. A class below the minimum fails. A class with no coverage fact fails too, unless its name ends in Test or _Test. Those are treated as test classes, and the detail says how many.
  • pass when every class is at or above the minimum.

docs.title: destructive_needs_label
docs.text:
Configured as policy.rules.destructive_needs_label with a label and optional tiers. An empty tiers list covers every tier.

  • skipped when it is not set, or the target's tier is not covered.
  • fail when the tier is unknown, or the facts do not say how many destructive changes the plan has.
  • pass when the plan has no destructive changes.
  • With destructive changes: fail when no pull request was found, or the pull request lacks the label. pass when it has the label.

docs.title: separation_of_duties
docs.text:
Configured as policy.rules.separation_of_duties with tiers and an optional approval. It makes sure the person who deploys is not the author of the change.

  • skipped when the rule is not set.
  • waived_by_config when the target's tier is not in tiers. An empty tiers list turns the rule off everywhere, because every tier is then outside the list.
  • Enforced when the tier is in tiers. The author is the pull request author and the deployer is the CI actor, compared without regard to case.
    • With no approval configured, it passes when both are known and differ, and fails when either is unknown or they are the same.
    • With an approval configured, it passes when they differ. When they are the same or unknown, it looks for a configured approval and gives satisfied_by_approval, or fail when none is found.

Two kinds of approval can satisfy the rule:

Mechanism Configured as Counts when environment approval.environment The run has an approved review for that environment label approval.label and approval.approvers The pull request has the label, and the person who added it is one of the approvers

A label approver may be the pull request author. The explicit approval by a listed approver is the control.

The PERMIT's separation_of_duties block records the result. Its mode is enforced, waived_by_config, satisfied_by_approval or not_applicable (the rule is off, or the PERMIT is an ephemeral automatic one). It also holds the author, the deployer and, for an approval, the mechanism and approver.

docs.title: analyzer_max_severity
docs.text:
Configured as policy.rules.analyzer_max_severity, a whole number from 1 to 5, where 1 is the worst.

  • skipped when it is not set.
  • skipped when there are no analyze facts, because the analyzer did not run. This is the one place a missing fact does not fail: a limit with no analysis behind it is not enforced until analysis exists.
  • fail when the facts show any violations at the configured severity or worse.
  • pass otherwise.

docs.title: Configuration example
docs.text:
version: 1
provider: salesforce
targets:
  prod:
    id: 00D000000000000
    tier: prod
    branch: main
    auth: { method: jwt, username: $SF_PROD_USERNAME, client_id: $SF_CLIENT_ID, key: $SF_JWT_KEY }
policy:
  permit_ttl: 2h
  windows:
    prod:
      - { days: [tue, thu], from: "18:00", to: "22:00", tz: America/Chicago }
  blackouts:
    - { from: "2026-12-20", to: "2027-01-03", tiers: [prod], reason: holiday freeze }
  rules:
    coverage_min: 85
    destructive_needs_label:
      label: destructive-ok
      tiers: [prod]
    separation_of_duties:
      tiers: [prod]
      approval:
        environment: glassops-deploy
    analyzer_max_severity: 2
salesforce:
  test_level:
    prod: RunLocalTests
  deploy:
    quick: prefer

permit_ttl is a duration from 5 minutes to 24 hours. The default is 2 hours.

docs.title: Evidence gate reads from GitHub
docs.text:
Some rules need facts that only GitHub knows. When the CI is GitHub and a token is available in GITHUB_TOKEN or GH_TOKEN, gate reads them through the GitHub API. Without a token it reads nothing, the facts stay absent, and the rules that need them fail. The ephemeral automatic PERMIT makes no API calls. GITHUB_API_URL overrides the API address.

Read Used for Token permission GET /repos/{repo}/pulls/{number} on a pull_request run Pull request author and labels pull-requests: read GET /repos/{repo}/commits/{sha}/pulls on a push The merged pull request for the commit, its author and labels pull-requests: read GET /repos/{repo}/actions/runs/{run_id}/approvals Environment approvals for this run actions: read GET /repos/{repo}/issues/{number}/events Who added the approval label, only when approval.label is configured and the pull request has it issues: read

On a push, the actor is GITHUB_ACTOR, the person who pushed or merged. A push that was not merged from a pull request has no author, and a rule that needs one fails. A call that fails adds an evidence.ci.* failure, so gate denies and exits 2.

The job also needs contents: write for deploy, because it pushes the glassops/deployed/<target> tag. Without it the deploy still succeeds and only the tag push warns.

docs.title: Platform Reference
docs.text:
The runtime this page once described was replaced by the glassops CLI. The GitHub Action inputs and outputs that were listed here no longer exist.

For the commands, flags, exit codes and result files, see the CLI reference. For the signed PERMIT and the policy rules, see PERMIT and rules. For architecture, see overview.md.

docs.title: GlassOps examples
docs.text:
consumer/ is the smallest repository layout that runs GlassOps on GitHub. Copy it into a Salesforce DX project, or run glassops init to generate a similar glassops.yaml and workflow.

  • glassops.yaml: two targets, a policy for production, and the default pipelines.
  • .github/workflows/pr.yml: runs the pr pipeline on pull requests by calling the reusable workflow.
  • .github/workflows/deploy.yml: runs the deploy pipeline on a push to main by calling the reusable workflow. The job runs in the glassops-deploy environment.

docs.title: Set up the environment
docs.text:
1. Create the glassops-deploy environment in the repository settings.
  2. Add the required reviewers, and a deployment branch rule that allows main only.
  3. Add GLASSOPS_PERMIT_KEY as a secret of that environment, not of the repository. Generate the value with openssl rand -base64 32. The deploy workflow passes it by name to the reusable workflow, which resolves it from the environment of the deploy job, because a called workflow gets an environment secret only when the caller passes it.
  4. Add the Salesforce secrets SF_JWT_KEY, SF_CLIENT_ID, SF_USERNAME, SF_DEVHUB_ORG_ID, SF_PROD_USERNAME and SF_PROD_ORG_ID as repository secrets.

The pr workflow never receives the permit key. Only a job in the protected environment can read it. The GitHub deploy guide explains each part of the deploy job.

docs.title: Other commands in a workflow
docs.text:
The glassops-platform/glassops action runs one command in the container, for steps that do not fit a pipeline:

- uses: glassops-platform/glassops@v1
  with:
    command: doctor --auth --target prod
    env: |
      SF_JWT_KEY
      SF_CLIENT_ID
  env:
    SF_JWT_KEY: ${{ secrets.SF_JWT_KEY }}
    SF_CLIENT_ID: ${{ secrets.SF_CLIENT_ID }}
